nameStory: The lily leaf beetle gets its name from its brilliant scarlet-red color and its preferred diet of lily plants. It's sometimes called the 'scarlet lily beetle' or 'red lily beetle' for the same reason - that unmistakable bright red shell that makes it stand out like a tiny fire engine on green lily leaves.
description: The lily leaf beetle is a small, bright red leaf beetle about the size of a ladybug that feeds exclusively on lilies and related plants. Its entire body is covered by a glossy, fire-engine red shell that's hard to miss against green foliage. These beetles are voracious eaters that munch on lily leaves, stems, buds, and flowers, often causing significant damage to garden lilies. Despite their small size, they can quickly strip a lily plant bare if left unchecked.

idTips.label: Brilliant red coloration
idTips.description: The entire beetle is a vibrant scarlet red color with a glossy, almost metallic sheen that catches the light - much brighter and more uniform than a ladybug's red

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About 6-8mm long (roughly the size of a pencil eraser) with an oval, slightly elongated body that's distinctly beetle-like rather than round

idTips.label: Host plant preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near lily plants, fritillaries, or other members of the lily family - if you see a small red beetle on a lily, this is likely your culprit

idTips.label: Feeding damage
idTips.description: Look for irregular holes chewed in lily leaves, often with dark, slimy larvae covered in their own excrement nearby

idTips.label: Movement behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, they often drop from the plant and play dead, or make a distinctive squeaking sound when handled

habitat: You'll find lily leaf beetles wherever lilies grow in New England gardens, parks, and naturalized areas. They're most common in suburban gardens and botanical collections where ornamental lilies are planted, but can also be found near wild lilies in woodland edges and meadows. They prefer sunny to partially shaded locations where their host plants thrive.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from soil and leaf litter where they overwintered, appearing on lily shoots as they emerge from the ground. This is when you'll first spot the bright red adults of the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are feeding, mating, and laying orange-red eggs on leaf undersides. Slimy, dark brown larvae covered in excrement appear and cause the most damage to plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves before winter. Late-emerging larvae pupate in the soil, while adults seek overwintering sites in leaf litter and garden debris.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected spots like leaf litter, mulch, and garden debris. No beetles are visible above ground during the coldest months.

funFact: Lily leaf beetle larvae cover themselves in their own slimy, dark excrement as a defense mechanism - this disgusting 'fecal shield' makes them so unappetizing that most birds and predators won't touch them, giving them nearly complete protection while they devour your lilies!
confusionNotes: The bright red color might make you think of ladybugs at first glance, but lily leaf beetles are much more elongated and lack the black spots that most ladybugs have. Remember: red and round with spots = helpful ladybug; red and oval without spots on a lily = destructive lily beetle.
contextualKnowledge: This beetle is actually a relatively recent arrival to North America, first discovered in the eastern United States in the 1940s and spreading rapidly since then. It's native to Europe and Asia, where natural predators help keep it in check, but here in New England it has few natural enemies and can be quite destructive to lily gardens.
compareHints: The lily leaf beetle is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify. Other red leaf beetles in the region are typically much smaller or have different color patterns, and none share its exclusive preference for lily family plants. Its combination of bright red color, moderate size, and lily-eating habits makes it quite distinctive among New England's leaf beetles.
